Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:54: Now I shall tell you what was told of one of the pious ones. They said that a certain pious man was once asked, which day of your life did you rejoice most? He answered: once I was traveling on a ship with merchants carrying fine merchandise, and in order to be alone with my Creator I went down to the stern of the ship and lay there in the lowest part; and one of the young merchants arose and disgraced me before his eyes, and spat in my face, exposed himself, and urinated on me — and I was astonished at his brazenness, but by the life of the LORD, my soul was not grieved at all by his deed. And when he passed from before me, I rejoiced with great joy that my soul had reached this measure of humility, for I knew from it that it had made progress among those who stand [in this virtue], for it had mastered this quality to the point that it felt nothing at all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:55: Our Sages of blessed memory have already said (cf. Sotah 5a) that these merit resurrection, as it is written (Isaiah 26:19), "awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust" — one who has already become dust in his lifetime. This refers to one who does not feel the disgrace of man, and therefore [the prophet] said, "but My salvation shall be forever."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:56: Now, his saying "those who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My Torah" is not, in my view, a mere repetition of the same idea, but a sign indicating with whom he speaks — namely, believers in [divine] providence. This is because it is known that two men standing before a judge to argue their case do not disgrace one another; and if this should happen, the insulted one remains silent and is pleased about it, since the disgrace of his adversary and the wickedness of his heart will be revealed before the judge. Therefore he said "those who know righteousness," for he believes in providence, and that the Master of the whole earth hears the words of the one disgracing him, and will repay him into his own bosom, and will answer on his behalf, leaving it to the true Listener who examines the hearts of men and knows the matters, whether for good or the opposite. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:57: With these words we can understand what we say at the end of our prayer, in "My God, guard my tongue from evil" etc., "and to those who curse me let my soul be silent" — for at first glance it would have sufficed to say "let me be silent," so why "my soul"? And likewise afterward it returns and says, "and let my soul be like dust to all." Rather, the intent is to inform us that lowliness should be embedded in the soul in such a way that the soul itself is the one that is silent — for it is possible that one might not respond to his own disgrace while still harboring hatred stored in his heart, as in (Genesis 27:41), "and Esau harbored a grudge against Jacob, and Esau said in his heart, let the days of mourning for my father draw near" etc. — and the verse says (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart," even if the pride remains only in the heart and is not expressed with the mouth. Therefore it says "let my soul be silent" — that the soul itself, of its own nature, be silent — this being along the lines of "in whose heart is My Torah" as the pious author, of blessed memory, explained, and the parable of the man dwelling in a city whose merchants are princes, etc.; and we likewise explained in the Gate of Love that all pride and anger come only from the side of matter, since the soul's own nature is to be lowly before the Creator and before all, as Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Exodus 16:7), "and what are we?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:58: He further says, "and let my soul be like dust to all" — explaining what is meant by "let my soul be silent": how is it possible for the soul to be silent and not feel it? It is that it be already so accustomed to receiving disgraces, like dust, which is prepared to receive people's constant trampling upon it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:59: The sage, the honored Rabbi Avraham HaLevi, may his light shine, said that we should learn the attribute of humility from dust — for dust, as long as it is coarse, is of no use for a craft, all the more so for making a vessel from it, and the more it is ground the better it becomes; so too with a person. And I say that this is why it says "and let my soul be like dust to all" — the more it receives disgraces, the more its soul is elevated.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:60: I found that Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz, may his light shine, wrote regarding "and to those who curse me let my soul be silent," an explanation as I have written. And regarding "and my soul like dust," he wrote: and not this alone, but that he should clothe himself in a garment of humility to the point of resembling his Creator, against whom people sin while He does good to them, as in (Nehemiah 9:20), "yet You did not withhold Your manna from their mouth" on the day they said, "these are your gods, O Israel" (cf. Exodus 32:4) — therefore it says, "and let my soul be like dust to all," for all trample it, yet it brings forth for them grain, bread, and food. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:61: Similarly, the aforementioned pious author wrote regarding the Mishnah "be not quick to anger" (Avot 2:10) — an interpretation fitting the verse (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools" — which relates to this exposition: for fools, because their anger is quick and they are fast to anger, anger dwells with them as though it made its home there; but with the wise man it does not rest, but rather immediately passes; and the reason for "bosom" is that their anger is hidden and they do not reveal it. Thus far the summary of his words. And this is "and to those who curse me let my soul be silent," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:62: Further there he gives another interpretation of this verse, along the lines of the interpretation "in whose heart is My Torah" that we have written, and says regarding the Mishnah "if I am not for myself, who is for me?" (Avot 1:14), in the name of Rabbi Yosef ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory. He further wrote that this sage was said never to have become angry in his life, and this was because he was never idle enough to become angry, being occupied with the pursuit of the life of the soul — and over what would he become angry, for all kinds of anger and rage come from concern for the body? Therefore he [Isaiah] said, "listen to Me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My Torah, fear not the disgrace of man," as we have already explained; therefore it says "anger rests in the bosom of fools," for their hearts are devoid of intellect and therefore anger takes hold. How honorable is their statement, "whoever becomes angry is as though he worships idols," indicating that his thoughts are far from his own essence. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:63: There are further matters fitting to consider so as not to become angry, and we shall explain them in a separate chapter, to give some space between chapters:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:1: The great reason preventing anger, hatred, and envy from the heart is when a person considers in his mind fulfilling the commandment (Leviticus 19:18), "love your fellow as yourself," which is a positive commandment encompassing several other commandments, as is said in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 31a), regarding that convert who came to convert before Hillel and said to him, teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot — and he said to him, "love your fellow as yourself: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow." When a person considers this, he will not disgrace his fellow nor insult him, just as he wishes for himself that no one disgrace him; likewise he will not respond to his own disgrace, just as, were the situation reversed and he were the one insulting, he would not wish to be responded to; and likewise he will judge his fellow favorably. And the commandments of not taking revenge and not bearing a grudge are commandments that, when a person fulfills them, he is necessarily compelled to overlook his own way and purify his heart of hatred entirely — thus, by the law of the Torah, a person is compelled to be humble.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:2: Since love of friends, the avoidance of strife, and the pursuit of peace are causes that bring a person to humility, I saw fit to copy here the chapter on love of friends that Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote in his book Menorat HaMaor. These are his words: "you shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall not take revenge nor bear a grudge" etc. (Leviticus 19:17-18). Our Rabbis taught: "you shall not hate your brother" — one might think he may not strike him or curse him but may hate him — the verse teaches, "in your heart" — the verse speaks of hatred that is in the heart. And we learn in tractate Yoma (23a): it was taught, what is revenge and what is grudge-bearing? Revenge: one says to him, "lend me your sickle," and he says, "no." The next day the other says to him, "lend me your axe," and he says, "I will not lend to you, just as you did not lend to me." This is revenge. And what is grudge-bearing? He says to him, "lend me your axe," and he says, "fine — I will not act as you did in not lending to me," [but lends it anyway while harboring the grudge].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:3: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says, love peace and hate strife, for even idol-worshippers, so to speak, are not touched by [divine judgment] when they are at peace, as it is said (Hosea 4:17), "Ephraim is joined to idols, leave him alone"; but if there is strife among them, what does it say of them? (ibid. 10:2), "their heart is divided, now they shall bear their guilt."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:4: It was taught (cf. Masechet DeRabbi Eliezer Zuta 9): a house in which there is strife will eventually be destroyed, and the Sages say strife in a city brings bloodshed to the city; a synagogue in which there is strife will eventually be destroyed, and some say it will eventually be scattered [its congregation dispersed]. Two Torah scholars living in one city, and likewise two courts, between whom there is strife, will eventually die. Abba Shaul says, strife between courts is the destruction of the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:5: In three places the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave idolatry but did not forgive strife. One: in the days of the generation of Enosh, they began to worship idols, as it is said (Genesis 4:26), "then it was begun to call upon the name of the LORD" [interpreted as the beginning of idolatrous mixing of the divine Name into idol names], and He did not punish them until the generation of the Flood, when there was strife among them, and they stole and robbed one another, and He did not forgive them, as it is said (ibid. 6:13), "the end of all flesh has come before Me." Second: in the generation of the wilderness, when they made the golden calf, He forgave them, but when they came to strife He did not forgive them — for wherever you find "and they murmured," you find guilt attached there. And greatest of all was the strife of Korach, and therefore the Name dealt with Korach and his congregation beyond the letter of the law. Rabbi Berechiah said, come and see how harsh strife is — for an earthly court does not punish [capitally] unless one is thirteen years and a day old, and the heavenly court [does not punish] unless one is twenty, but here even nursing infants perished, as it is said (Numbers 16:29), "if these die the common death of all men" etc. Third: when the tribes divided over Judah and Benjamin and there was no peace between them, retribution came upon both — when the Ten Tribes sinned, the tribe of Judah came and punished them, as it is said (2 Chronicles 13:19), "and Abijah pursued Jeroboam and captured cities from him, Beit-El and its villages... and Jeroboam did not recover strength again in the days of Abijah, and the LORD struck him and he died" — and although Jeroboam worshipped idols, the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave him, until he divided against the tribe of Judah and was punished.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:6: Rabbi Meir says, strife is harsh, for even strife that is for the settling of the world — it is not said of it "that it was good"; in all the acts of creation it is said "that it was good," but regarding the separation of the firmament between the waters it is not written "that it was good" [since this created a division]. And is this not a kal vachomer: if strife that is for the settling of the world is not written with "that it was good," strife that is for the destruction of the world, how much more so [is it not to be called good].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:7: Strife is harsh, for it is equivalent to the generation of the Flood — it is said of Korach's congregation (Numbers 16:2), "chieftains of the congregation, summoned to the assembly, men of renown," and it is said of the generation of the Flood (Genesis 6:4), "who were of old, men of renown." Strife is harsh, for it brings mortal danger, as it is said (ibid. 13:12), "and he pitched his tent as far as Sodom" — because he separated from Abraham, he was close to being destroyed like Sodom, were it not for the merit of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, as it is said (ibid. 19:29), "and God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot" etc. Strife is harsh, for it brings death, as it is said (Exodus 21:22), "and if men strive together," and it is written, "and if there is a fatal injury" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:8: Rabbi Yitzchak says, three are called wicked: one who raises his hand against his fellow, one who is brazen-faced, and one who borrows and does not repay. That one who raises his hand [is called wicked], from where do we learn this? As it is said (Exodus 2:13), "and he said to the wicked one, why do you strike your fellow?" — it does not say "you struck" but "why do you strike," teaching that he had not yet struck him. That the brazen-faced one [is wicked], from where do we learn this? As it is said (Proverbs 21:29), "a wicked man makes his face brazen." That one who borrows and does not repay [is wicked], from where do we learn this? As it is said (Psalms 37:21), "the wicked one borrows and does not repay." From where do we learn that it is forbidden for a person to strike his fellow? As it is said (Deuteronomy 25:3), "forty he may strike him, he shall not add" — and is this not a kal vachomer: if regarding one who has been sentenced to lashes we are commanded to strike him no more than the [permitted] lashes, then a person striking his fellow, how much more so [is it forbidden]. From where do we learn that it is forbidden to provoke one another? As it is said (Deuteronomy 2:19), "and when you draw near opposite the children of Ammon, do not harass them" etc. — and is this not a kal vachomer: if regarding Ammon and Moab, of whom the verse says (ibid. 23:7), "you shall not seek their peace or their welfare," it is nevertheless said, "do not besiege them and do not provoke them," then Israel toward one another, how much more so.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:9: Hatred is so harsh that it destroyed the Temple, as we learn in Gittin (55b) — through Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, Jerusalem was destroyed etc.; see there. And there Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said, come and see the power of shame — for the Holy One, blessed be He, assisted Bar Kamtza and destroyed His own house and burned His sanctuary [rather than let the shame of that man go unavenged].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:10: Jerusalem was destroyed for the sin of baseless hatred, and this is supported by [the verse] (Lamentations 1:1), "*Eichah *yashvah *badad *ha'ir" ["how does the city sit solitary"], whose initial letters spell "eivah" [enmity]. And we learn in Yoma (9b): it was taught, in the Second Temple period, when they were expert [in Torah] and occupied with Torah and acts of loving-kindness — why was it destroyed? Because of the baseless hatred that was among them — to teach you that baseless hatred is equivalent to idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed [combined]. And our Sages of blessed memory said (there), "for the bed is too short to stretch out on" (Isaiah 28:20) — what is "too short to stretch out"? That two evils cannot fit together [at once, i.e., the sins of the First Temple and this new one of baseless hatred].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:11: Most of the sufferings that come upon a person come from the sin of baseless hatred, as we learn in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 32b): it was taught, Rabbi Nechemiah says, for the sin of baseless hatred, strife comes into a person's house, his wife miscarries, and his sons and daughters die while young.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:12: We learn in Avot D'Rabbi Natan (cf. 16:1): Rabbi Yehoshua says, an evil eye, the evil inclination, and hatred of one's fellow creatures drive a person from this world and from the World to Come — for whoever hates his fellow, the Holy One, blessed be He, uproots him from the world; for so we find with the people of Sodom, who were uprooted only because they hated one another, as it is said (Genesis 13:13), "and the men of Sodom were evil" etc. — "evil" to one another, and "sinners" through forbidden relations, "to the LORD" through idolatry, "exceedingly" through bloodshed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:13: We learn in the Mechilta: "when you see the donkey of your enemy" (Exodus 23:5) — if you subdue your inclination to make your enemy your friend, I promise you that you will make your enemy your friend, as it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him." And the sage said, one enemy should be in your eyes like a thousand thousands of thousands of enemies, while a thousand thousands of thousands of friends should be in your eyes like one. And although baseless hatred is a great sin, a person is nevertheless obligated to hate the wicked, just as he is obligated to love the companions who walk in the straight path, as it is said (Psalms 139:21), "do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:14: Another interpretation: "when you see the donkey of your enemy" — if regarding one who hates him the Torah says this [to help], how much more so regarding one who does not hate him. And David, peace be upon him, called the enemy by four terms of disgrace: violence [chamas], baseless [chinam], falsehood [sheker], emptiness [reikam]. "Violence," as it is said (Psalms 25:19), "see my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with violent hatred" — these are those who hate the judges, acquitting the guilty and convicting the innocent in pursuit of violence. "Falsehood," as it is said (ibid. 38:20), "and my enemies are vigorous and many; those who hate me falsely have multiplied," "their deceit is falsehood" (ibid. 119:118) — these are those who hate the upright because they speak truth, while they themselves seek to speak falsehood, calling evil good and good evil. "Emptiness," as it is said (ibid. 25:3), "let the treacherous be ashamed, empty" — these are those who hate Torah scholars who say there is judgment and there is a Judge, as though it were fitting to say the world is empty [of justice]. "Baseless," as it is said, "and words of hatred surrounded me, and they fought against me without cause [chinam]" (ibid. 109:3) — these are those who hate their fellows for no reason, as it is said (ibid. 59:5), "without iniquity they run and prepare themselves; awake to help me and see."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:15: A person should always love his fellow creatures — this commandment is a positive commandment, as it is said (Leviticus 19:18), "love your fellow as yourself." A person is obligated to love his fellow and be concerned for his wealth, as we learn (Avot 2:12), Rabbi Yosi says, let your fellow's money be as precious to you as your own — and our Sages of blessed memory explained: just as a person watches over his own money, so he should watch over his fellow's money, and just as he would not spread a bad name about his own money, so he should not spread a bad name about his fellow's money. If he sees his fellow in a place of danger, he is obligated to save him with all his ability, and if he does not save him, the verse considers it as though he killed him, as it is said (Leviticus 19:16), "do not stand by your fellow's blood," and our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 73a): if you see your fellow drowning in a river, or bandits coming upon him, you are obligated to save him, as it is said, "do not stand [by]" etc. And it is written (Proverbs 24:11), "save those taken to death" etc.; and should you say, who sees me, why should I endanger myself, "peace be upon my own soul" — the verse teaches (ibid. 24:12), "if we say, 'behold, we did not know this' — does He who weighs hearts not perceive it? He who watches over your soul knows it." And if he saves him, it is as though he had sustained an entire world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:16: Even if it is his enemy or one who hates him, he is obligated to save him, as it is said (Exodus 23:5), "when you see the donkey of your enemy" [struggling]. And whoever does so, the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased with his deeds, as it is said (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways" — meaning, if he wishes that the Holy One, blessed be He, be pleased with his way, let him himself repay good even to his enemies. How so? If he sees his fellow's ox or donkey lying under its burden, he should help him raise it up — immediately his enemy will remove the hatred from his heart, and for this the Holy One, blessed be He, will be pleased with his way. And it was taught: one who has adversaries [does something] from above, as we learn (Avot 3:10), anyone with whom the spirit of the creatures is pleased, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:17: A person should always associate with the good and the upright, and distance himself from the company of the wicked and worthless people, as we learn (Avot 1:7), Netai the Arbelite says, distance yourself from a bad neighbor, and do not associate with the wicked — and our Sages of blessed memory explained (Avot D'Rabbi Natan 9:1): [this refers to] a neighbor in the house, a neighbor outside, and a neighbor in the field — for tzara'at afflictions come only upon the house of that wicked person, and cause the destruction of the wall of the righteous man [next to him]. How so? If the wall between a wicked man and a righteous man has an affliction appear in the wicked man's house, they demolish the righteous man's house because of the wicked man's affliction. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, says, woe to the wicked man, woe to his neighbor — the wicked man's sins caused the destruction of the righteous man's wall.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:18: Another interpretation: "do not associate with the wicked" (there, 9:4) — a person should not associate with an evil man, for Jehoshaphat associated with Achav and went up with him to Ramoth-Gilead, and wrath came out against him, as it is said (2 Chronicles 19:2), "should you help the wicked?" etc. — and again he associated with Achaziah, and the LORD broke his works, as it is said (ibid. 20:37), "because of your association with Achaziah, the LORD has broken your works." We likewise find with Amnon, who associated with Yonadav, who gave him evil counsel, as it is said (2 Samuel 13:3), "and Amnon had a friend named Yonadav" etc., who was clever for evil purposes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:19: We learn in Avot D'Rabbi Natan: if the young men say to you, "come, let us build the synagogue," do not listen to them; but if the elders say to you, "come, let us tear down the synagogue," listen to them — why? Because the building of the young is [like] destruction, and the destruction of the elders is [like] building. Proof of this: the counsel of Rechavam ben Shlomo, who abandoned the counsel of the elders and took the counsel of the young men [and it led to disaster].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:20: Do not be a companion to a wicked man, even for matters of Torah, but rather a person should strive to acquire a good companion and distance himself from a bad companion, as we learn in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 25): "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (Proverbs 13:20) — to what is this comparable? To one who enters a perfumer's shop — even if he takes nothing and gives nothing, he acquires a good scent; so too, whoever walks with the righteous acquires their ways and their good deeds. "But the companion of fools shall be broken" — to what is this comparable? To a person who enters a tannery — even if he takes nothing and gives nothing, he acquires a bad odor; so too, one who walks with the wicked acquires their ways and their deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:21: The author [of Menorat HaMaor] said: a parable — to what is this comparable? To two men walking on a road who encountered two groups of people also traveling on the road. In the first group were righteous, upright, God-fearing men. One of the two travelers joined them, and whoever saw him with them thought he was one of them; when they reached the city, he separated from them and entered the city, and they continued on their way. In the second group were worthless men, thieves and murderers, who robbed the possessions of whomever they found on the road. The second traveler joined them and walked with them, and whoever saw him on the road thought he was one of them; when they reached the city, he separated from them and entered the city, and they continued on their way. Now, two men came to the city, both from that same city [as residents]. One of them had seen the group of righteous men, and that man among them, and told the people of the city, "I saw on the road a group of holy pious men, and I pleaded with them to enter the city so that the people of the city might honor them, but they were unwilling." While he was speaking, behold, that man who had joined them on the road and separated from them near the city passed by. He said, "this man is from that group of righteous men." Immediately they showed him great honor and appointed him as their head — all this because he had joined the good. The second traveler had seen those thieves and robbers as he approached the city, and was immediately alarmed and feared for his life and hid until they passed; and once he entered the city, he told the people of the city, "I saw on the road a gang of thieves who were killing whomever they found and plundering their money." While he was speaking, behold, that man who had joined them on the road and separated from them near the city passed by. He said, "this man is from that gang of thieves." Immediately they seized him and hanged him — all this because he had joined the wicked, even though he had not stolen or plundered with them — and he died an unnatural death. Thus far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:22: Whoever wishes to distance himself from transgressions should distance himself from the company of the wicked. The sages of ethics said, when you wish to inquire about a person, ask with whom he associates, for every person acts like his fellow; therefore a person should associate with the good and distance himself from the company of the wicked and evil. The sage said, the company of the good is honor and glory, while the company of the vile is shame and disgrace. And one who associates with the good is like one who carries musk — even if he gives none of it to his fellow, his fellow still benefits from it [by the scent]; and one who associates with the wicked is like a person near a burning furnace — even if he is not burned, he will still be scorched. They further said, one never associates with the wicked and parts from them in peace.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:23: Always, every kind attaches to its own kind — the righteous man attaches to the righteous, and the wicked man attaches to the wicked, as it is said (Leviticus 11:15), "every raven after its kind."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:24: We learn in Bava Kama (92b): people have a saying, a bad palm tree goes and walks toward a nest of ravens [i.e., migrates toward similarly worthless trees/company]. Meaning: the bad palm tree that produces no fruit joins the barren trees that produce no fruit, and is glad among them. This matter is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah (Genesis 28:9), "and Esau went to Ishmael." Repeated in the Prophets (Judges 11:3), "and worthless men gathered around Jephthah." Tripled in the Writings, "every bird dwells with its own kind, and man with his like" — though this last is not in Scripture but in the Book of Ben Sira, and he said "in the Writings" loosely, since it is written [there, in that book].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:25: Whoever wishes to know his fellow's character should observe what he praises — if he praises good qualities, he is known to be a person of good qualities, and if the opposite, the opposite; this is what is written (Proverbs 27:21), "the crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, and a man is [tested] by his praise" — he praises only according to his own qualities, whether bad or good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:26: There are six things a person cannot do [without consequence], and these are they: first, there is no person who pursues the fulfillment of his desire's craving without sinning. Second, there is no person who constantly converses with women without coming to adultery. Third, there is no person who gathers much money whose heart does not become proud because of it. Fourth, there is no person who associates with the wicked and parts from them in peace. Fifth, there is no person who draws close to kings without the times eventually turning against him. Sixth, there is no person who requests anything from base people whose request is granted [without cost to himself]. But the company of the good is entirely beneficial without harm, even if they give him nothing of their own, and even if they do not intercede on behalf of their companions — nevertheless their company is good and beneficial, since people honor them; therefore a person should associate with the good. The sage said, whoever associates with the good, his own level and his family's level will rise; whoever associates with the wicked will eventually become like them; and a wicked man who associates with the righteous will eventually become like them, as it is said (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise." A person should always be a servant to the generous and the good, rather than a ruler or judge over the base and the lowly, as we learn (Avot 4:15), be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:27: Rabbi says, when Lot went to Abraham our father, peace be upon him, he learned from his ways and his good deeds. What did Abraham do? He made a guesthouse in Charan, and whoever entered he would feed and give drink, and say to him, "the God of Abraham our father, blessed be His name, is One"; and when Lot arrived, he did likewise.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:28: The sage further said, it is not fitting for a wise man to associate with a person until he has examined whether he is fit for companionship or not. He further said, companionship concerns four matters, and the love of companions is comparable to food. First is a person's companionship with his wife and children, of which it is said (Proverbs 5:19), "be intoxicated always with her love" — and just as a person always needs food, by which his body's existence is sustained, so is a person's companionship with his wife and children always [needed], just as every day he needs to see them, and through them he has quiet, tranquility, and settled peace of mind. And from where do we learn that a person's wife and children are compared to food? As it is said (Psalms 128:3), "your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children like olive saplings" — comparing the wife and children to a set table. Second is [companionship] comparable to medicine — this is the companionship of a brother, for just as a person needs medicine only at the time of illness, so the companionship of a brother is needed only at a time of distress and trouble, as it is said (Proverbs 17:17), "and a brother is born for adversity." Third is the companionship of good friends, whose love and compassion are compared to a father's compassion for his son — of a father it is written (Malachi 3:17), "as a man has compassion on his son who serves him," and it is written (Psalms 103:13), "as a father has compassion on his children"; and of a friend it is written (Job 19:20), "have pity on me, have pity on me, you my friends." Fourth is [companionship] comparable to deadly poison — this is the companionship of the wicked, the evil, and worthless people, for just as deadly poison harms and kills, so friends [of this kind] harm and kill.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:29: We learn in the Midrash: whoever associates with a wicked person robs himself of this world and the World to Come. Whoever shows a pleasant face to a wicked person is among those who provoke God. Whoever deceives mourns in his own body [i.e., suffers physical consequence]. Whoever turns his fellow from the good path to the bad path dies in the midst of his days. Whoever mocks the commandments is shown no mercy from Heaven. And whoever habitually reddens his fellow's face [causes him public shame], his ledger is open that very day, etc., as is stated in "the pearl of Rabbi Meir," which we copied in the Gate of Awe, chapter 12.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:30: There are fifteen things a good companion must do for his faithful friend, and then his companionship will be fitting and complete without deceit, and these are they: 1) He should greet him first. 2) He should invite his companion to all his good occasions. 3) And on his day of celebration. 4) He should keep his secret and not reveal it. 5) He should be his helper at a time of his trouble. 6) He should visit him in his illness and strive to attend to his needs all the days of his illness. 7) He should occupy himself with the matters of his burial if he dies. 8) He should correct his words to his face, all the more so not behind his back. 9) He should overlook all the wrongs he has done him and forgive him immediately. 10) He should rebuke him if he knows he has done wrong. 11) He should honor him immediately. 12) He should not deceive him in business dealings. 13) He should do everything he has vowed to do for him. 14) He should not lie to him. 15) He should always seek mercy for him and seek his good in his heart.
